# AI literacy, educational level, and parenting self-efficacy of children’s education among parents of primary school students

### _Keywords:_ Parenting self-efficacy, representing parents’ confidence in their capability to effectively handle parenting re-

AI literacy sponsibilities and obstacles, is an important determinant of parenting quality. Parents’ educational level is Parenting self-efficacy known to be an important predictor of parenting self-efficacy. Nowadays, children are exposed to Artificial In- Parenting

telligence (AI) from an early age, especially in their learning process. Parents’ AI literacy emerges as an 

Educational level

important factor that could contribute to parenting self-efficacy of children’s education. However, no previous studies have investigated how parents’ AI literacy is related to parenting self-efficacy. The quantitative study examined the associations among parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and parenting self-efficacy of children’s education. Data were collected from 160 parents of primary school students in Hong Kong through online sur- veys. Results showed significant relationships among parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and parenting self- efficacy of children’s education. The association between parents’ educational level and parenting self-efficacy was partially mediated by the subfactors of AI literacy. The study extended the literature by investigating AI literacy from the parents’ side and highlighted the importance of parents’ AI literacy in parenting regarding children’s education. It had implications for practitioners and policymakers to develop intervention programs to 

help parents improve AI literacy.

According to Belsky’s \[[11\]](#appendix-b) determinants of parenting model, parenting is influenced by three domains, which are parental, child, and socio-contextual factors. Among these three domains, parental factors have the greatest impact on parenting, both in direct or indirect ways through social contexts and children \[[11\]](#appendix-b). Empirical studies have examined various parental factors that influence parenting, such as parents’ educational levels \[[12\]](#appendix-b). Previous research suggests that par- ents’ educational level is significantly related to PSE \[[12,5\]](#appendix-b). For example, mothers with higher educational attainments tend to feel confident in parenting and be better parents \[[13\]](#appendix-b). Parents with higher educational levels are more likely to seek out parenting knowledge and perceive greater social support than less-educated parents, which may help to increase confidence in their parenting roles \[[12\]](#appendix-b).

However, with the growing prevalence of technology in children’s education, emerging parent-related factors like parents’ AI literacy should be considered in research on parenting. Parents with higher levels of AI literacy skills might be more confident in parenting children in terms of their educational development. Understanding parents’ AI literacy can inform educational policies and intervention programs which aim to help parents use AI in parenting in the AI-driven society, thus improving patents’ parenting confidence and efficiency in chil- dren’s education. Investigating AI literacy from the perspective of par- ents may also provide novel insights in technology designs for developing user-friendly AI tools for parents in parenting. Even though AI literacy has been a heated topic in recent years, research on AI literacy in the educational field mainly focuses on stu- dents’ and teachers’ AI literacy \[[14–22\]](#appendix-b), such as developing AI literacy curricula in schools to help children gain AI knowledge \[[23\]](#appendix-b), and investigating students or teachers’ perspectives of AI literacy education \[[24,25\]](#appendix-b). To the best of our knowledge, no prior studies have investigated parents’ AI literacy, let alone its relationship with parents’ educational level and PSE. Therefore, the study aimed to make contributions to the existing knowledge of parents’ AI literacy and its relationship with PSE of children’s education and parents’ educational level. By exploring AI literacy from the perspective of the parents, the study sought to fill the gap in the literature by providing insights into understanding parenting in the digitalized society.

### _1.1._ _Parenting self-efficacy (PSE)_

As a construct developed from Bandura’s \[[26\]](#appendix-b) social cognitive the- ory, self-efficacy is defined as an individual’s beliefs about his or her ability to perform a task or achieve a goal \[[27\]](#appendix-b). People with higher levels of self-efficacy tend to be more persistent in completing tasks \[[28\]](#appendix-b). PSE refers to parents’ confidence in their abilities to successfully raise a child \[[1,](#appendix-b)29\]. It includes the level of a parent’s knowledge about the behaviors related to children’s development and how to raise a child, as well as the level of parents’ confidence in their capability to confront the parenting role without frustration \[30\].

PSE is regarded as closely related to parenting behaviors, which means that parents with higher self-efficacy are more likely to use a variety of supportive strategies to raise a child and are more affectionate in parenting, such as being sensitive to children’s feelings or needs \[[1,](#appendix-b) 29,31\]. Previous studies show that PSE is also related to children’s be- haviors and general development. For instance, Malm et al.’s \[32\] study examined the relationships between PSE and bullying of students at the elementary level, and it found that parents’ higher level of PSE was related to a lower possibility of children’s violence and bullying. Junttila and Vauras \[[3\]](#appendix-b) investigated PSE among subgroups of fathers, mothers, and couples, and they found that there were significant relationships between PSE and children’s social behaviors, indicating that children with parents of stronger PSE tended to show higher levels of social competence.

Higher self-efficacy in parenting is also associated with parents’ increased engagement in home learning activities, such as reading, and 

parents’ guidance in doing homework \[33,[27\]](#appendix-b). Additionally, there is also research that pays particular attention to PSE and children’s learning outcomes, but there are mixed results. Albarran and Reich’s study \[[4\]](#appendix-b) suggests that infant mothers’ self-efficacy about childcare activities is positively associated with children’s language skills at around 18 months. However, later studies conclude that parents’ gen- eral feeling of self-efficacy in parenting is not directly related to chil- dren’s vocabulary development \[[27,](#appendix-b)34\]. The inconsistency of the result might be explained by the idea of Sti´evenart and Martinez Perez \[29\] that parents’ cognitions, like self-efficacy, have an influence on parents’ behaviors and then consequently affect children’s early language development.

In addition to research highlighting the importance of PSE, some studies pay attention to the predictors influencing PSE. It is suggested in the literature that child factors like behavior problems could influence parents’ PSE. For instance, parents whose children have more aggressive behaviors are more likely to have weaker PSE \[35\]. In addition, parental factors are widely covered in studies investigating the predictors of PSE. It is suggested that educational level, as a parental factor of the three dimensions of Belsky’s \[[11\]](#appendix-b) parenting model, has a significant influence on PSE \[[12\]](#appendix-b). Parents who are better educated are more eager to gain knowledge about parenting and get more social support in raising a child, thus perceiving higher levels of confidence in parenting \[36\]. However, the influence of educational level on PSE might be indirect, but very few studies have investigated the indirect relationship between these two factors.

Moreover, Coleman and Karraker \[[2\]](#appendix-b) indicate that PSE is a multilevel concept including general PSE, domain-related PSE, and task-related PSE. Except for the investigation of general PSE, more attention should be paid to the PSE of specific domains such as children’s edu- cation. As mentioned before, parents’ self-efficacy is related to their behaviors and engagement, and Epstein \[37\] suggests that parents’ involvement not only includes creating a learning environment for children at home but also encompasses getting knowledge of school programs, school decision-making, and children’s learning progress at school. Therefore, parents’ beliefs about their ability to influence their children should be unpacked in research, but limited attention has been paid to the specific domain of parents’ self-efficacy regarding children’s education and school learning.

### _1.2._ _AI literacy_

With the development of technology, artificial intelligence (AI), which is referred to as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines” (\[38\], p. 2), is gradually integrated into human’s daily lives. AI literacy is then put forward to describe the capability to comprehend the fundamental methods and concepts of AI in various products and services \[39\]. Some researchers relate AI literacy to the skills required to critically evaluate, communicate, and work with AI \[40\], and also associate it with skills, confidence, and readiness to acquire AI knowl- edge \[41\]. Casal-Otero’s \[42\] systematic review suggests that AI literacy could be defined as skills that enable individuals to understand AI through three aspects, which are gaining knowledge of AI, learning how AI works, and learning for life with AI. Similarly, in Chiu et al.’s \[43\] study, AI literacy is regarded to cover multidimensions, including knowledge of AI, readiness to use AI, beliefs of the relevance of AI, and attitude towards AI.

AI literacy is put forward to strengthen the significance of adding the AI concept to digital literacy skills for individuals, including children \[44\]. Although the important role of AI literacy is gaining popularity in educational studies, most research is confined to the school context and pays attention to the AI literacy of children \[[14,15,](#appendix-b)45,[19,22\]](#appendix-b). Some research focuses on the role of AI literacy education in children’s AI knowledge gaining and how to integrate AI into the curriculum in classrooms to reach educational aims. For example, Su and Yang’s \[[22\]](#appendix-b) intervention study indicated that young children could gain 

fundamental concepts and knowledge about AI from an AI literacy program, which suggested the positive influence of AI literacy education on children’s understanding of the changeable technological world. Some studies also provide suggestions for educators from the pedagog- ical perspective, such as developing some collaborative, hands-on pro- jects using AI in order to connect children’s understanding of AI concepts and AI applications \[[17\]](#appendix-b). A recent study by Su \[[21\]](#appendix-b) focused on teachers’ beliefs of AI literacy education and found that more than half of the teachers in the research confirmed the importance of children’s AI literacy education in the classroom, and there still existed challenges to promoting AI literacy education, including insufficient support from the institution and curriculum, as well as teachers’ inadequate knowledge of AI literacy and children’s incomprehensive abilities.

Very limited studies focus on AI literacy in the home environment. Druga et al.’s \[46\] study investigated parents’ role in children’s AI lit- eracy development at home. The result suggested that parents could have many roles, including cheerleader, mediator, and collaborator in the joint digital learning processes, and family had the potential to be the third space for children’s AI literacy development. Nowadays, par- ents should recognize their responsibilities, seize opportunities, and deal with the challenges of raising a child in digital environments \[[6\]](#appendix-b). The important role of parents’ knowledge of AI technologies could be considered in the digital parenting process. However, parents’ AI liter- acy has drawn scarce attention from scholars in the educational field. Although Su’s \[[10\]](#appendix-b) recent study investigated AI literacy from the par- ent’s perspective, she mainly focused on parents’ attitudes toward AI education in kindergartens but did not investigate parents’ AI literacy skills. Rahayu and Haningsih \[[23\]](#appendix-b) conducted research to explore the digital competence of mothers in Indonesia, and they found that family SES could predict mothers’ digital competence in parenting. The study looked into the digital literacy skills of parents and investigated the relationship between family characteristics and parents’ digital literacy skills, but the study focused on digital competence in a broad way without involving AI literacy.

Although AI literacy has been an increasingly popular topic in recent years, most studies focus on the AI literacy of K-12 students and teachers \[[14,15,18–20,39,45\]](#appendix-b). How parents’ AI literacy influences parenting in the digital age should also be investigated. Parents with high levels of AI literacy might feel more confident and have more PSE regarding chil- dren’s education in an AI-driven society, but to our knowledge, no studies have investigated the association between parents’ AI literacy and their PSE. Studies on AI literacy should go beyond children’s AI knowledge and try to link parents’ AI literacy to their self-efficacy in terms of children’s education.

### _1.3._ _Parents’ educational level_

Family socioeconomic status (SES), which is mostly based on the measurement of parents’ educational level, parents’ occupation, and family income \[47\], is known to have an influence on children’s development \[48\]. Compared with family income, which is related to material resources, parents’ education is regarded as a more powerful predictor of parental behaviors and beliefs \[48\], and it is also suggested to play a stronger predicting role in children’s academic development than other contextual factors like parents’ occupation \[49\]. Parents’ educational level could shed more light than other family characteristics on the influence of family SES on children’s development in educational and psychological studies \[49–51\]. Parents with higher educational levels are more able to find good jobs and create more material resources for the family. In other words, parents’ education drives their occupa- tion and the family income \[48\]. Parents’ education plays an important role in creating a context that enriches the family and helps parents gain knowledge of the importance of children’s educational development \[48\].

Parents’ educational level is closely associated with parenting, such as parents’ beliefs about parenting and their specific practices in child- 

rearing. Higher education attainment enables parents to explore and evaluate the information in raising a child and pay attention to the child’s well-being \[52\]. Parents from better educational backgrounds tend to be more careful about their children’s development in parenting, and they have relatively higher expectations for children’s educational achievement \[52\]. They are also more likely to spend more time developing home activities with their children \[53\]. In addition, they pay more attention to their communication with children in parenting. For example, it is indicated that parents with a college degree are more confident than those without a college degree in responsibly commu- nicating with their children regarding media use \[[5\]](#appendix-b).

Empirical studies suggest that parents’ educational level is related to their PSE. For example, Coleman and Karraker’s \[30\] research examined the relationship between maternal characteristics and mothers’ PSE, and the result suggested that mothers with better educational background had more self-efficacy in raising a child. Similarly, Peacock-Chambers et al.’s \[54\] study, which explored the associations between socio- demographic factors and PSE, suggested that parents with post-high school educational levels showed higher levels of PSE. While former studies indicate a close relationship between parents’ educational level and PSE, the relationship between them might not be direct. However, very few studies have investigated the potential factors influencing the relationship between parents’ educational level and PSE especially specific domain of PSE regarding children’s education, and the path- ways of the relationship between them should draw attention from researchers.

### _1.4._ _The present study_

#### _1.4.1._ _Parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and PSE_

In the digital era, children are exposed to AI technologies like Siri from an early age and grow up in environments filled with various intelligent technologies. AI has gradually shown its prevalent role in children’s educational development, and chatting robots for language learning might be one of the examples. Given the highly digital envi- ronment where children are raised, parents nowadays should be equipped with AI literacy skills to feel efficacious in guiding them in digital learning. However, to our knowledge, no research has investi- gated the relationship between parents’ AI literacy and PSE. Lim \[55\] conducted a study to examine the relationship among digital literacy, self-efficacy, and perspectives on children’s AI education of teachers, and the result showed that these three factors were positively correlated with each other, suggesting that improving teachers’ digital literacy and self-efficacy was highly needed in order to guide teachers in using AI in the school environment. Lim’s \[55\] study highlighted the importance of teachers’ digital literacy and self-efficacy in this AI-driven society. Similarly, parents’ AI literacy and self-efficacy are also important in children’s development nowadays, and we hypothesize that parents with higher levels of AI literacy might be more efficacious in parenting children regarding their educational development.

Additionally, parents’ educational level as a demographic feature has a significant impact on PSE \[[12\]](#appendix-b), and it is also closely associated with their views towards technology \[56\]. Gessulat et al.’s \[[5\]](#appendix-b) study investigated the relationship between family characteristics and PSE, and the result suggested that parents with fewer educational attainments need more support in developing PSE. Parents with a university degree were more confident in taking the responsibility to communicate with their children regarding media use \[[5\]](#appendix-b).

It is suggested that parents with higher educational attainments might more actively look for information on parenting and may feel they have greater social support compared to parents with lower education levels \[[12\]](#appendix-b). Parents who are knowledgeable about digital devices including AI technologies can guide children to take advantage of the positive aspects of the technology while also noticing its risks and negative sides \[[6\]](#appendix-b). Previous studies suggested that teachers equipped with more digital literacy skills have higher levels of self-efficacy \[55\]. 

Similarly, it is hypothesized that parents with higher AI literacy skills may have higher levels of PSE regarding children’s education. There- fore, the hypothesized model of the present study is put forward as follows in [Fig. 1:](#142-research-questions)

Existing literature has mentioned the close relationships among the subdimensions of AI literacy. For instance, AI readiness, AI relevance, and AI knowledge are significantly associated with each other among primary school students \[57\]. However, each subfactor may have its unique contributions regarding children’s learning behaviors and educational outcomes. For example, general knowledge of AI can improve children’s confidence in using AI tools, while AI readiness may be related to their engagement when using AI technologies \[57\]. In addition, the well-known framework of TPACK (Technological Peda- gogical Content Knowledge) for teachers’ digital competence \[58\] and the emerging model of TAICS (Teacher AI Competence Self-efficacy) evaluating teachers’ AI competence \[[24\]](#appendix-b) both adopt multi-faceted approach, suggesting that multiple dimensions of knowledge are important for effective teaching practices or learning processes. While these models were developed for educators, they are theoretically adaptable to parenting, given that parents serve as the first teachers in children’s development \[59\]. In today’s AI-driven educational context, unpacking parents’ AI literacy into distinct subdimensions allows for a more in-depth understanding of how each facet may influence parenting self-efficacy.

Theoretically, perceived preparedness plays a critical role in shaping self-efficacy beliefs \[60\]. AI readiness, reflecting perceived prepared- ness, may activate parents’ behavioral engagement with AI technolo- gies, which foster their self-efficacy in parenting practices. From a cognitive perspective, AI knowledge equips parents with the ability to critically assess and utilize AI tools in their children’s development, thus enhancing their perceived competence in parenting \[60\]. In addition, Fidan and Olur’s \[61\] study suggests that parents’ attitudes towards digital parenting is significantly related to digital parenting self-efficacy. Parent’s attitudes towards AI, reflecting their affective orientations, can shape their willingness to adopt AI in parenting practices thus may in- fluence their PSE. Moreover, people’s perceived relevance to using technology influences their motivation and confidence to use technol- ogy \[62\]. Parents with higher AI relevance might be more likely to use AI technologies in parenting regarding children’s education and thus have higher PSE in today’s context where AI is prevalent in children’s educational development. Therefore, in light of the reviewed theories and prior empirical studies, the present study treats the subfactors of parents’ AI literacy independently to gain an in-depth understanding of their different roles in parenting regarding children’s education. We hypothesize that the four dimensions of AI literacy are significantly related to PSE and the conceptual figure is provided in [Fig. 2.](#22-measures)

#### _1.4.2._ _Research questions_

Based on the conceptualization of the constructs stated above, the study aimed to investigate the associations among parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and PSE of children’s education. The study focused on 

**Fig. 1.**

the specific domain of PSE regarding children’s education. The study was guided by the following research questions: (1) Are parents’ AI literacy and its subfactors, including AI knowledge, AI readiness, AI relevance and AI attitude, educational level, and PSE of children’s ed- ucation, significantly related to each other? Based on the literature discussed above, we hypothesized that there would be significant posi- tive associations among AI literacy, educational level, and PSE. (2) Do parents’ subfactors of AI literacy (i.e., AI knowledge, AI readiness, AI relevance, and AI attitude) significantly mediate the relationship be- tween parents’ educational level and PSE of children’s education? We expected that AI literacy would be a significant mediator between par- ents’ educational level and PSE. The conceptual model in [Fig. 2](#22-measures) articu- lates mediational hypotheses later tested by the path analysis. In order to address these questions, the next section details the methodological approach including participants, measures, data collection and data analysis methods.

## 2. Methodology

### _2.1._ _Participants_

According to the 2020 Census report of the Hong Kong Census and Statistics Department \[63\], nearly 78 % of households in Hong Kong are equipped with personal computers, indicating that digital devices have been integrated into people’s daily lives. For children in Hong Kong, digital technologies are widely used both in the school contexts and in the home environments. Regarding AI, Hong Kong plays a leading role in the development of AI technologies, and the Hong Kong government pays high attention to the usage of AI technologies in the educational fields \[[22\]](#appendix-b).

In recent years, with the development of technology, AI has gradu- ally emerged as a popular topic in Hong Kong and is also exposed to children throughout their everyday lives. Children learn to communi- cate with Siri and other chatting robots or AI assistants on digital devices like cell phones and tablets from an early age. It is pointed out that digital devices, as an integral part of daily life in Hong Kong, influence parenting practices \[64\]. Therefore, the widespread use of AI technology may also impact parenting on children’s education, and Hong Kong parents with higher levels of AI literacy might feel more efficacious in children’s learning in an AI-driven world. Based on the reasons shown above, Hong Kong was chosen as the context for the present study. Before the participants recruitment, a priori calculation of sample size was conducted using G\*Power, based on an effect size of 0.15, with a conventional power of 80 %, a two-sided hypothesis test, and an alpha level of 5 % \[65\]. The analysis indicated that a minimum of 92 partic- ipants was required for the study. Ultimately, the participants of the study were composed of 160 parents including 124 mothers and 36 fa- thers of P4–6 children from 7 Hong Kong local schools. Parents of stu- dents of P4–6 were chosen as the target participants because AI has gradually integrated into formal learning at primary schools, especially for children in higher grades \[66\]. ### _2.3._ _Data collection_

Data collected in this study is part of a larger study on an online English learning platform. We adopted convenience sampling, which involves recruiting participants who are accessible and willing to participate in the study \[[16\]](#appendix-b). Although convenience sampling might cause self-selection bias, its advantages including ease of implementa- tion and cost-effectiveness make it a suitable sampling strategy for the present study, which targets at parents \[[16\]](#appendix-b). Surveys can offer numerical data and can be analyzed in a straightforward way \[72\]. Online surveys are welcomed nowadays because they are cheap, fast, and efficient \[72\]. The online survey provides a good approach for data collection in the present study because the target participants of the study were parents and they are normally busy. Therefore, the online survey was adopted as the data collection method in the study. Each participant completed the survey independently and anonymously, with no repeated measures or clustering, ensuring independence of observations. Parents’ participa- tion was on a voluntary basis. As an incentive, 60 participants were selected randomly and rewarded with a supermarket cash coupon or online tutorial class for their children. The survey took around 20–30 min to complete. The data collection of parent survey took approxi- mately 3–4 months.

parents’ educational level and PSE. Different from correlation analysis, 

path analysis focuses on causal links between a set of variables, and it is basically an extension of multiple regression \[77,78\]. However, it can look at both direct and indirect effects that could not be achieved by regression analysis. It can provide an examination of the causal re- lationships among variables by enabling them to function as both in- dependent and dependent variables \[79\]. It also helps to assess the strength of the relationships and to test the significance of the hypoth- esized causal relationships between the variables \[78,80\], which aligns with the aim of the study. Because the hypothesized model in the present study was fully constrained, the traditional model fit was not reported, and we mainly focused on the path estimates of the model and the proportion of variance accounted for to address the research questions. In the path model, parents’ educational level was posited as the pre- dictor of PSE, with the four subfactors of AI literacy, including AI knowledge, AI readiness, AI relevance, and AI attitude, as the mediators. Having outlined the methodological approach of the study, the following section will present the results and findings obtained from applying these methods to the sample.

## 3. Results

Participants’ demographic information is presented in [Table 1.](#22-measures) In terms of educational level, the largest group was the parents with a high school degree, representing 35.0 % of the total participants. 0.6 % of the participants had a primary school degree or held a doctoral degree, representing the least portion of the whole population. Regarding the age distribution of the participants, most parents were aged from 36 to 40 years old, comprising 34.4 % of the participants. There were no parents from the age group of 21–25, 26–30, and 56–60, and only one parent was above 60 years old.

[Tables 2 and 3](#23-data-collection) show the descriptive statistics of the variables and the simple correlation result. Regarding normality, all the variables in this study meet the criterion reported in 2.4. We opted for Spearman cor- relation analysis due to the ordinality of the indicators, such as the educational level, and for robustness against local deviations or nonlinear relationships. Consistent with the hypothesis, the Spearman correlational analysis suggested significant relationships among par- ents’ educational level, AI literacy, and PSE of children’s education.

sought to understand the associations among parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and PSE of children’s education. The results indicate that parents’ educational level is positively related to PSE regarding children’s learning. Parents with better educational backgrounds are likely to be more efficacious in parenting children in their education, which aligns with the findings of previous research \[[2,5\]](#appendix-b). Parents with higher educational attainments might be more actively engaged in getting knowledge of parenting and perceive fewer difficulties in parenting a child, thus gaining a higher level of PSE \[36\]. The findings of the study also confirm Belsky’s \[[11\]](#appendix-b) determinants of parenting model by addressing the importance of parents’ factors in parenting. However, the result is inconsistent with the findings of some previ- ous studies suggesting a null relationship between parents’ educational level and PSE \[81,82\]. One reason might be the different focus of par- ents’ self-efficacy between the current study and these studies because the present study mainly concentrates on PSE regarding children’s ed- ucation instead of investigating PSE in a general way. Another reason might be that the target participants of these studies are parents of in- fants or pre-school-aged children, while the current study focuses on the parents of primary school students. PSE is important in the processes by which parents utilize effective practices in response to children’s development over time \[[26\]](#appendix-b), which means that a developmental view should be adopted regarding PSE. The association between family fac- tors and PSE may also vary in the process of children’s development. Therefore, further studies can adopt a longitudinal method to gain a more in-depth investigation into the relationship between the educa- tional level PSE over time.

Regarding the relationship between parents’ educational level and AI literacy with its subfactors, the findings indicate a significant result. Parents with a higher educational degree are likely to be equipped with more AI knowledge and have more positive attitudes towards AI tech- nologies, which is similar to the findings of previous studies on teachers’ educational levels and technological skills \[83\]. The finding is also consistent with Rahayu and Haningsih’s \[[23\]](#appendix-b) study, suggesting that family SES, including parents’ educational level, can predict mothers’ digital competence in parenting even though AI elements are not involved in their study. In addition, the study indicates that parents with higher levels of AI literacy tend to show more PSE in their children’s education. As reviewed earlier, very little attention has been paid to parents’ AI literacy in previous studies. Therefore, the current study extends the literature by exploring the important role of parents’ AI literacy in parenting in terms of children’s education.

Another interesting finding of the study is that the association be- tween parents’ educational background and PSE is partially mediated by the four subfactors of AI literacy. Among the four dimensions of AI lit- eracy, AI readiness is the only significant mediator in the relationship between parents’ educational level and PSE in the path model, which implies that the degree to which parents feel equipped and ready to work every day with technology with integration of AI is especially important in converting their educational background into higher PSE. Parents with higher educational levels can get easier access to AI re- sources and higher readiness to use AI technologies, making them more confident in using AI when parenting children regarding their learning. In contrast, AI knowledge, AI relevance, and AI attitude are not identi- fied as significant mediators, which indicates that while gaining knowledge of AI, understanding it, and having a positive attitude toward it might be important, being practically prepared to utilize AI is more significant for improving PSE.

The results revealed a comparatively high average level of AI literacy among the participants, with all subscales scoring above the midpoint. This might be attributed to Hong Kong’s prominence in technological development. Therefore, caution is needed when generalizing the results to less digitalized regions. However, the observed ceiling effect in AI literacy provides another explanation for why AI readiness emerged as the sole significant mediator. With limited variance in AI literacy among this tech-savvy population, AI readiness, the most practice-oriented 

factor, becomes the primary mediator influencing PSE. At the same time, the results offer a pragmatic lesson for the design of future parent- training programs on AI technologies. These programs should prioritize the translation of existing AI familiarity into practical competence and confidence, rather than simply focusing on conveying the basic AI principles. By emphasizing practical application with the aid of readiness-oriented workshops or materials for families, the training programs can effectively utilize parents’ existing AI knowledge to enhance their parenting self-efficacy and improve children’s educa- tional outcomes.

This emphasis on practical application aligns with cultural values in many Asian regions, including Hong Kong. In these contexts, children tend to be submissive and obedient to parents and teachers \[84,85\]. Chinese parents, in particular, are often actively involved in their chil- dren’s education and hold high expectations for their academic perfor- mance \[86\]. These cultural values may further influence their attitudes toward technology, especially the use of digital tools in parenting and supporting children’s learning. Indeed, previous studies suggest that individuals in Eastern cultures may be more inclined to depend on AI tools compared to people in the Western because of the emphasis on self-efficacy and autonomy in individualistic Western cultures \[87\]. This cultural preference for using technologies, together with the high AI literacy in our sample, highlight the need for parent-training programs to prioritize practical application. In addition, it is important to take cultural values into consideration when designing AI literacy programs for parents in terms of supporting children’s education. For further studies, cultural frameworks should be drawn to investigate parents’ AI literacy and parenting across different cultures to contextualize findings. Based on the result, the association between AI readiness and PSE deserves further investigation, particularly by exploring the potential pathways through parental behaviors, given the abundant empirical evidence highlighting the significant impact of parental behaviors on PSE \[[1,](#appendix-b)29,31\]. Additionally, even though AI knowledge, AI relevance, and AI attitude are suggested to be insignificant mediators in the rela- tionship between parents’ educational level and the PSE of children’s education, these null findings warrant further interpretation. One possible explanation for AI knowledge being the nonsignificant media- tors may be that parents possess a foundational understanding of AI concepts but may not translate this knowledge into effective parenting practices that enhance PSE. Regarding AI relevance, it is possible that parents perceive the relevance of AI but still struggle to integrate AI into practical education support for children. As for AI attitude, while par- ents may hold positive attitude towards AI, but they are not sufficient to influence PSE. These three subdimensions of AI literacy may influence PSE through various factors related to parenting practices, as well as other contextual influences, which deserves further exploration in future studies. The results suggest that the observed relationships in the path analysis are consistent with our hypothesized model, but it is important to acknowledge that the cross-sectional nature of the data allows for statistical inferences rather than causation.

To our knowledge, there has been no prior study examining the importance of parents’ AI literacy and its multidimensions in the rela- tionship between parents’ educational level and PSE. The research adds novel insights by providing an overview of the direct and indirect pathways through which parents’ educational level influences PSE and highlights the unique role of AI readiness in developing PSE in children’s education. The study also makes contributions to the investigation of parents’ AI literacy in the Hong Kong context. As mentioned above, Hong Kong is a leading region in the development of technologies in education, both in the academic field and in the implementation of educational technology. The current study fills the gap in exploring the important role of Hong Kong parents’ AI literacy in parenting children in education. The cultural and linguistic adaptation of the PSE scale and the improved internal consistency methodologically contribute to further investigations in the field of parenting. In addition, given the exploratory nature of this research in the emerging area of AI, our 

findings provide foundation for future studies and theoretical develop- ment regarding AI and parenting. Moreover, the study has significant practical implications for policymakers and educators that interventions and training programs are highly needed to help parents enhance AI literacy, especially the sense of readiness in using AI technologies in parenting children regarding education. Merely focusing on and assessing parents’ AI knowledge, AI attitude and AI relevance is not sufficient to improve their parenting self-efficacy.

### _4.2._ _Limitations and possible directions in further studies_

Some limitations of the study should be addressed. First, the study adopted a cross-sectional approach and captured the data only in a single time point, which could not suggest causal relationships among variables. PSE is reflected in the processes of parenting practices \[[26\]](#appendix-b), so a developmental view should be adopted in the investigation of PSE, and further studies may explore the predictors of PSE in a longitudinal way. Second, the research adopted a self-report method to measure parents’ AI literacy. AI literacy testing scales should be developed to accurately evaluate different dimensions of AI literacy. Additionally, the AI literacy scale adopted in the present study was initially designed for students \[43\]. Although the scale was suggested to have good reliability in the present study, AI literacy skills for parents and students may have different focuses due to their different ages and roles. Therefore, further studies should develop a scale specifically assessing parents’ AI literacy. Moreover, while the original scales have been used in previous studies in the Chinese context \[70,71\], the translation between English and Chi- nese may affect the results. Although systematic steps were taken to ensure the translation accuracy, more rigorous methods, including cul- tural equivalence testing, should be adopted to further validate the translation of the scale in future studies.

Another limitation should be mentioned here is the generalizability of the study. Although we specifically focused on parents of students of P4–6 instead of parents of children in all primary school levels, parents of older children in higher grades, especially the transitional grade to middle school (i.e. P6), might feel differently about their ability to help children in digital learning compared to parents of younger children. Further studies can explore variations in PSE among parents of children across different grade levels and age ranges. In addition, the sample was predominantly female, with approximately 77 % of participants being mothers. This gender imbalance may be due to mothers often being the primary caregivers and more actively involved in children’s education \[88\]. However, it limits the generalizability of the findings to fathers. In addition, while the study included participants with varying levels of education, the distribution of educational levels is not representative enough for the whole population of Hong Kong, which also limits the study’s generalizability. Another point is that due to the strong tech- nological development of Hong Kong where the study was conducted, the findings reflecting the local sample might not be generalized to less tech-savvy regions.

Furthermore, only parents’ educational level is included in the study as the family characteristics predicting parents’ AI literacy and PSE. Other potentially relevant demographic variables such as parental occupation, family income, and parent-child relationship (i.e., father or 

## Appendix A

Items of parenting self-efficacy of children’s education in English

mother), were not included as control variables in the model, which might confound the relationship between AI literacy and PSE. Addi- tionally, convenience sampling was adopted in the study, which might generate self-selection. Therefore, further replications should incorpo- rate some demographic control variables in the model. Further study may also compare the AI dimensions across different sociodemographic groups and go beyond the Hong Kong context integrating cultural frameworks. Finally, while AI readiness is the only significant mediator in the association between parents’ educational level and PSE, further studies may expand the path model by exploring other possible path- ways. Practically, the study points out the important role of AI literacy in parenting in Hong Kong, and governments and educators should consider developing training programs to help parents develop AI lit- eracy. Therefore, intervention studies will be highly needed to develop inclusive and efficient AI literacy programs.

## 5. Conclusion

Building upon the discussion of the findings within the context of existing literature, we can now make a conclusion. The present study investigated the associations among parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and PSE and examined the mediating role of AI literacy in the relationship between parents’ educational level and PSE of children’s education. The result suggested that parents’ AI literacy, educational level, and PSE were significantly associated with each other. The find- ings of the study also indicated that the relationship between parents’ educational background and PSE was partially mediated by the four subfactors of AI literacy, among which AI readiness was the only sig- nificant mediator. The study extended the literature by investigating AI literacy from the perspective of parents and also highlighting the importance of parents’ educational levels and AI literacy in parenting in terms of children’s learning. Importantly, the study focused on parents’ AI literacy and its link to PSE, which was underexplored in previous research. Moreover, transparency of the study, such as the detailed in- formation on normality criteria and data cleaning, as well as the adap- tation of the PSE scale and its high reliability after refining, methodologically contributed to further investigations in the field of parenting.
